blocks.text: Treating viral infections is fundamentally different from treating bacterial ones. Bacteria are independent living organisms, while viruses are parasites that are not truly alive on their own: they live inside our cells and use our own DNA/RNA machinery to replicate. This makes it hard to develop a drug that kills the virus without harming our healthy cells.

blocks.title: Mutation
blocks.text: Viruses can change their genetic material very quickly; this is called mutation. A drug that works against a virus one year might not work the next, because the virus has changed. This is why flu vaccines need to be updated every year.

Some viruses also integrate into our genome or stay inactive ('asleep') in our cells for years, and present drugs can kill only active viruses. Antiviral medicines work by targeting specific stages of the viral life cycle: some prevent the virus from entering our cells, while others stop the virus copying its genetic material. One of the most common mechanisms is enzyme inhibition. For example, a protease inhibitor does not allow the virus to cut the protein it produces in one long strand into working proteins. These inhibitors also help in the treatment of HIV and hepatitis C infections. Some antiviral drugs strengthen the immune response instead; interferons are proteins that boost the immune system to fight viruses.
